data_points.claim: A rainbow needs two things at once: sunlight coming from behind the observer and water droplets somewhere in front of them; the sun must sit lower than about 42 degrees above the horizon for a full bow to clear the ground.
data_points.source_name: NOAA NESDIS — What Causes a Rainbow?

data_points.claim: Inside each droplet the light path is refraction on entry, a single internal reflection off the back of the drop, then refraction again on exit — without that internal reflection there is no rainbow, only transmitted light.
data_points.source_name: UK Met Office — Rainbows: optical wonders

data_points.claim: Colors separate (dispersion) because each wavelength has a slightly different refractive index in water: violet light is bent the most and red the least, so the droplet acts like billions of tiny prisms working in concert.
data_points.source_name: Scientific American — Why do rainbows form instead of just straight bands of colors?

data_points.claim: The primary bow's geometry is fixed by geometry of minimum deviation: red light emerges at about 42 degrees and violet at about 40 degrees from the antisolar point, which is why red is always on the outer edge and the bow spans only ~2 degrees of sky.
data_points.source_name: University of St Andrews School of Physics — Rainbows (optics treatment)

data_points.claim: A rainbow is centered exactly on the antisolar point — the spot directly opposite the sun, which sits below the horizon — so the bow is always a complete circle; the ground simply hides the lower half, which is why full-circle rainbows are only seen from planes, drones, cliffs, or mountaintops.
data_points.source_name: Chandra / Smithsonian — Somewhere Over The Rainbow

data_points.claim: Every observer sees a slightly different set of droplets, so the rainbow you see is unique to your exact eye position — no two people, even standing side by side, ever see the same rainbow.
data_points.source_name: Scientific American — Why do rainbows form?

data_points.claim: A secondary bow is produced by light that reflects twice inside each droplet; it appears above the primary, is much fainter, has its colors reversed, and sits at a radius of about 51 degrees, with Alexander's dark band — first described by Alexander of Aphrodisias around 200 AD — occupying the unlit sky between the two bows.

misconceptions.myth: A rainbow is a fixed object sitting out there at a particular place in the sky.
misconceptions.reality: It is an optical illusion tied to your eye position; as you move, the droplets forming your bow change, so it moves with you and can never be approached.
misconceptions.source: Scientific American — Why do rainbows form?

misconceptions.myth: A rainbow has exactly seven colors.
misconceptions.reality: It is a continuous spectrum; the seven-color division was imposed by Isaac Newton, partly to mirror the seven notes of the musical scale.

misconceptions.myth: You can walk to the end of a rainbow and find the pot of gold.
misconceptions.reality: Because the bow is centered on the antisolar point below the horizon and is observer-dependent, it has no physical 'end' to reach.
misconceptions.source: NOAA NESDIS — What Causes a Rainbow?

misconceptions.myth: It has to be raining on you to see a rainbow.
misconceptions.reality: The rain just needs to be in front of you while the sun is behind you; a rainbow is often seen against a storm that is moving away.
misconceptions.source: UK Met Office — Rainbows: optical wonders

audience_insights.knowledge_level: Most viewers already know a rainbow involves rain plus sunlight and can list 'seven' colors, but very few know the decisive geometry — that it is always a full circle centered on the antisolar point, that the sun must be below ~42 degrees, or that their rainbow is unique to their eyes. Those three ideas are the fresh 'aha' payload.
pain_points: Explanations stop at 'light bends in water' without ever connecting it to the shape of the bow in the sky.
The reversed colors and faintness of the double rainbow are shown but never explained.
Viewers lose interest in dense ray-tracing diagrams that don't tie back to what they'll actually see.

expert_voices.name: Theodoric of Freiberg
expert_voices.title_or_affiliation: Dominican friar and natural philosopher, c. 1304
expert_voices.position: Gave the first essentially correct explanation of the rainbow, tracing light through a water-filled glass sphere to show refraction, internal reflection, and refraction again.

expert_voices.name: Rene Descartes
expert_voices.title_or_affiliation: Mathematician and philosopher, Discourse on the Method (1637)
expert_voices.position: Quantitatively ray-traced millions of light paths through a raindrop to derive the rainbow's ~42-degree cone.

expert_voices.name: Alexander of Aphrodisias
expert_voices.position: First recorded the dark band between the primary and secondary bows — now Alexander's band — about 1,800 years before cameras could photograph it.

angles_discovered.hook: Every rainbow you've ever seen has been hiding its other half below the horizon.
angles_discovered.why_now: Drone and airplane footage of full-circle rainbows now circulates constantly on social media, so the 'it's a full circle' reveal lands as a fresh, visual surprise rather than a dry fact.

angles_discovered.name: Your Rainbow Belongs Only To You
angles_discovered.hook: No one else on Earth sees the exact rainbow you see — not even the person beside you.
angles_discovered.why_now: The observer-uniqueness fact is almost never the lead of rainbow content, yet it directly overturns the 'fixed object' misconception held by most viewers.

angles_discovered.name: The 1800-Year-Old Mystery Of The Dark Band
angles_discovered.hook: A Roman philosopher spotted a rainbow's missing light centuries before anyone could explain it.
angles_discovered.why_now: Alexander's band pairs a human story (Theodoric, Descartes) with a phenomenon viewers can test on the next double rainbow they see, giving a strong narrative spine.
grounded_in: secondary bow / Alexander's band data point

angles_discovered.name: Why The Second Rainbow Reads Backwards
angles_discovered.hook: The second rainbow in a double rainbow prints its colors in reverse — and there's a simple reason.
angles_discovered.why_now: Color reversal is one of the most-asked rainbow questions online, and the viral 'Double Rainbow' video proves audiences already care, so an explanatory payoff is guaranteed to land.

research_summary: The single most important insight is that a rainbow is not a fixed object at all: it is an observer-dependent, full-circle optical illusion centered on the antisolar point below the horizon, built when sunlight refracts, internally reflects, and refracts again inside billions of droplets at a locked 40-42 degree cone. Everything viewers find magical — the arc, the uniqueness to their eyes, the reversed double bow, the unreachable 'end' — falls out of that one geometric fact, which makes it the ideal spine for an explainer that converts awe into understanding.
